stem: A claims-triage step keeps a human reviewer because its outcome, loss ratio, surfaces in 12 months. Override rate is the readiness proxy; it rose from 4% to 11% this month. The director cites this proof and asks to remove review. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Reject the request: a rising override rate signals growing disagreement, not growing trust; investigate before automating further.
Approve removing review: the rising rate proves reviewers trust the model enough to intervene less.
Automate the step outright; it is high-volume and machine-readable, which already justifies full automation.
Replace the human reviewers with a more capable model, since fewer overrides would follow from better outputs.

whyRight: Override rate is a proxy for reliability; a rate that rose from 4% to 11% means reviewers are overriding more often, which is evidence against readiness, not for it. The director's reading inverts what the metric measures.

whyWrong.B: The stem states the rate rose, meaning reviewers intervened more often, the opposite of growing trust; reading a rising rate as proof of confidence inverts the evidence.
whyWrong.C: High volume and machine-readability are fit signals, but the section also requires correctness to be visible immediately; a rising override rate says it currently is not.
whyWrong.D: Swapping in a more capable model does not diagnose why disagreement is rising; it discards the review step's signal instead of investigating the cause behind it.

lessonKey: automating before disagreement further growing investigate override rate reject request rising signals trust

stem: A moderation pipeline outputs a JSON verdict with a confidence score for an automated router. A human panel now reviews cases below that threshold, and the chair says reviewers can't tell why a case was flagged. What should the panel's output include?

opts.t: Reasoning and citations alongside the verdict, since the panel is the consumer and must weigh the case.
The same JSON verdict and confidence score the router already receives, unchanged.
A full transcript of every intermediate reasoning step plus the raw input document, unfiltered.
The existing confidence score, with a stricter threshold so fewer cases reach the panel.

whyRight: The output consumer determines the shape of the contract; a human panel weighing borderline cases needs the reasoning and citations behind a verdict, not just the score already built for the automated router's routing decision.

whyWrong.B: The confidence score alone is what already reaches the panel; it is the reason reviewers cannot tell why a case was flagged, not a fix for it.
whyWrong.C: A full unfiltered transcript replaces a designed, shape-matched contract with a raw dump the panel must now parse itself, which is worse for a time-pressed reviewer, not better.
whyWrong.D: Raising the threshold changes which cases reach the panel; it does nothing about the output shape those cases arrive in, which is the stated complaint.

t1Clause: A human panel now reviews cases below that threshold

stem: An invoice-intake pipeline processes 100,000 documents a day. 96% arrive in one standard layout; 4% use formats the team hasn't catalogued yet, and those often need a step no prior document required. Which architecture should the team implement?

opts.t: An agent for every document, since it can adapt to any format without hardcoded rules.
A fixed workflow for the standard layout, routing anything unmatched to an agentic exception path.
A fixed workflow for the standard layout, sending anything unmatched to a human queue.
A single retrieval-augmented call that looks up the correct layout template before extracting fields.

whyRight: Matching each population to its cheapest rung serves both correctly: a fixed workflow handles the enumerable 96% at the lowest cost and highest testability, while the agentic exception route absorbs the 4% whose paths cannot be listed in advance.

whyWrong.A: An agent for every document pays nondeterminism and token cost on the 96% whose format is already known, to serve a requirement only the remaining 4% actually has.
whyWrong.C: A human queue handles the unmatched 4% but drops the stated requirement that those cases still need automated processing through some path, not a manual dead end.
whyWrong.D: Retrieval solves a missing-data lookup problem; it does not solve routing a request down an enumerable path versus an unlistable one, which is what the 4% requires.

t1Clause: 96% arrive in one standard layout; 4% use formats the team hasn't catalogued yet

stem: A coordinator already passes synthesis findings downstream as structured content-plus-metadata records, preserving source, document, and page for a regulated audit trail. A senior reviewer asks for a cleaner prose-only summary without the metadata block, calling it easier to read. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Keep the structured handoff as-is; a prose-only summary would remove the metadata the audit trail requires.
Treat this as a coverage gap: have the coordinator re-delegate targeted queries and re-invoke synthesis before responding.
Replace the structured handoff with the prose summary, and add a separate compliance review step to catch citation errors.
Replace the structured handoff with the prose summary the reviewer requested, since readability is the stated concern.

whyRight: The structured content-plus-metadata handoff already satisfies the citation and audit-trail requirement; a prose-only summary flattens content and provenance together, which is exactly the failure the passing format exists to prevent, regardless of how the request is framed.

whyWrong.B: Coverage gaps are a synthesis-completeness problem solved by re-delegating queries; this request is about output format and citation integrity, a different failure the coordinator did not cause.
whyWrong.C: A compliance review step can catch a citation error after the fact, but it does not restore the per-claim metadata the prose summary already discarded at synthesis.
whyWrong.D: Readability is the reviewer's stated preference, not the compliance requirement the handoff format exists to satisfy; the audit trail needs the metadata regardless of how the summary reads.

t1Clause: preserving source, document, and page for a regulated audit trail
lessonKey: audit handoff keep metadata only prose remove requires structured summary trail would

stem: A compliance-reporting pipeline splits into nine agent calls, one per data field, each seeing only the prior call's single output. The compliance officer reports increasingly conflicting figures across fields. A senior architect proposes splitting further, one call per field per source. Select two corrections.

opts.t: Merge steps back toward the point where each unit again shares the context that made figures consistent.
Stop splitting once each unit has one evaluation criterion and one failure mode, not a fixed field count.
Split further into one call per field per source, since finer granularity has historically improved reliability.
Keep the nine-call structure and add a final pass that reconciles conflicting figures across all outputs.

whyRight: The nine-way split has passed its stopping rule: units no longer share context, and conflicting figures are the direct symptom. Restoring shared context by merging, then re-splitting only where one evaluation criterion and one failure mode genuinely require it, fixes the cause rather than compensating downstream.

whyWrong.C: Splitting further multiplies handoffs and repeats the context loss already causing conflicts; the historical pattern cited does not hold once units share less, not more.
whyWrong.D: A reconciliation pass detects conflicting figures after they occur; it does not restore the shared context the split removed, so the same conflicts recur at the next report.

t1Clause: splits into nine agent calls, one per data field

stem: A workflow must meet a 3-second p95 latency commitment and hold cost down at 50,000 requests a day. It runs five serial steps including enrichment, and routes every case through the same full-size model regardless of difficulty. Select two independent fixes.

opts.t: Parallelize the independent steps only, leaving the enrichment step inside the request path untouched.
Keep the current serial chain unchanged, and add caching plus a monitoring alert for SLA breaches.
Move the enrichment step off the request path by precomputing it at ingest time.
Route by confidence tier and use the smallest model that clears the accuracy bar for routine cases.

whyRight: The SLA fails on serial depth; cost is driven by routing every case through a full-size model. Moving enrichment off the request path removes the SLA-breaking step, and confidence-tier routing with the smallest sufficient model removes the cost driver.

whyWrong.A: Parallelizing alone still leaves enrichment inside the request path, so the tail latency the commitment is written against keeps breaching; it also does nothing for cost.
whyWrong.B: Caching and an alert instrument the breach the serial chain keeps producing rather than removing its cause, and neither action lowers the per-request model cost.

t1Clause: and hold cost down at 50,000 requests a day
lessonKey: bar clears confidence enrichment ingest model move off path per plus precompute request routing smallest tier

stem: A VP sponsoring a drafting tool for renewal letters plans to judge success from user feedback after launch, without recording current handling time or turnaround days for the 40,000 letters processed yearly. What should the architect do first?

opts.t: Build the drafting tool now and gather user feedback after launch to see whether it helped.
Deploy the tool with usage dashboards and derive the baseline retrospectively from those logs.
Measure current handling time and turnaround days for renewal letters before committing to a design.
Skip baseline measurement and frame the rollout as a transformation success story instead.

whyRight: Turnaround and handling time are the units the business case will be judged in; without a recorded before, the launch cannot be shown to have helped even if it works, which is the exact failure the misconception invites.

whyWrong.A: Waiting for after-launch feedback captures no before figure; the improvement claim has nothing recorded to compare against.
whyWrong.B: Deployed system logs reconstruct downstream a measurement the pre-project step could have captured cleanly beforehand.
whyWrong.D: Renewal-letter drafting already exists as a human task, so an efficiency baseline applies; transformation framing is for capabilities that did not exist before.

t1Clause: for the 40,000 letters processed yearly (an already-existing, human-done process)

stem: A support system's citations became inaccurate after last week's document refresh; compliance relies on them for a regulated audit trail across 30,000 monthly tickets. Model version and prompt are unchanged. Which fix should the architect apply?

opts.t: Re-index and refresh the retrieval layer's embeddings so lookups reflect the newly published source documents.
Replace the underlying model with a more capable one, since it is the newest available version.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to double-check each citation before responding.
Capture the mismatched citations and route them into the evaluation set for future model tuning.

whyRight: The citations broke immediately after the document refresh while the model and prompt held steady, which locates the fault in the retrieval layer; re-indexing against the refreshed sources fixes the cause instead of the model or the prompt.

whyWrong.B: The model version did not change, so the model is not the failure point; replacing it does not touch the stale retrieval index causing the mismatch.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction asks the model to try harder; it cannot correct citations pointing at documents the index has not updated to reflect.
whyWrong.D: Model version and prompt are stated as unchanged, so this is not a tuning problem; routing it to the eval set delays the fix without touching the index.

t1Clause: the citations went wrong immediately after a scheduled document refresh

stem: A vendor-onboarding pipeline runs the same five checks for every submission across 2,000 vendors monthly, but one step reconciles an uploaded document set whose count, order, and naming vary unpredictably per vendor. How should that step be designed?

opts.t: Keep the other four checks fixed; give the reconciliation step an agent planning its approach per submission.
Extend the fixed pipeline's reconciliation logic to cover the most common document layouts seen so far.
Replace the entire five-check pipeline with one agent planning every step for each submission.
Route any submission with more than three documents to a human reviewer instead.

whyRight: Four of the five checks are enumerable and belong in a fixed pipeline, but the reconciliation step's shape is genuinely unlistable per vendor; giving only that step an agent buys adaptive planning where it is actually needed, and nowhere else.

whyWrong.B: Extending the template to the most common layouts covers the majority silently, but drops the vendors whose document sets do not match any listed shape.
whyWrong.C: The other four checks are enumerable and fixed by requirement; replacing them with agentic planning buys nondeterminism the stated task never asked for.
whyWrong.D: Sending the variable cases to a human reviewer abandons the automation requirement for exactly the population that needed a working design.

t1Clause: whose count, order, and naming vary unpredictably per vendor
lessonKey: agent approach checks fixed four give keep other per planning reconciliation step submission

stem: An expense agent extracts a vendor name from each receipt, and a downstream step needs that name to look up the approved spending category, across 50,000 monthly submissions with a 24-hour reimbursement commitment. How should the steps be orchestrated?

opts.t: Keep both steps in the current order but switch to a faster underlying model to shorten wall-clock time.
Dispatch both steps together from a single coordinator turn, since that is how independent subtasks are parallelized.
Chain the steps sequentially so the lookup runs only after extraction returns the vendor name.
Let both steps run as issued and add a monitoring check flagging any lookup with an empty vendor name.

whyRight: The lookup step cannot begin until it has the vendor name the extraction step produces, which is a real data dependency; sequential chaining is required, and issuing both in one turn would send an empty value downstream.

whyWrong.A: A faster model shortens each call but does not remove the dependency; the lookup still cannot run before extraction has returned a name.
whyWrong.B: Single-turn dispatch parallelizes independent subtasks; here the lookup depends on the extraction's output, so issuing both together sends the lookup an empty value.
whyWrong.D: Monitoring an empty vendor name after the call detects the failure but does not prevent it; the sequencing itself must guarantee the value exists first.

t1Clause: a downstream step needs that name to look up the approved spending category

stem: A claims-intake team must meet a stated six-hour acknowledgment SLA and hold cost per claim within a set ceiling as intake volume triples during renewal season. Which architecture should the team adopt?

opts.t: Route every claim through confidence-tier logic to the smallest model that clears the bar, minimizing cost per claim.
Keep the current pipeline and add an automated alert that escalates whenever the acknowledgment SLA is breached.
Parallelize the independent intake checks to meet the SLA, applying confidence-tier routing only to hold cost within the ceiling.
Replace the pipeline with a fully autonomous agent that decides each claim's routing case by case.

whyRight: The SLA is a stated commitment that filters designs before comparison; parallelizing removes the serial depth causing the miss, and confidence-tier routing keeps cost inside the ceiling. The pure cost-tier design meets cost alone and still breaches the commitment, which is the trap this facet targets.

whyWrong.A: Confidence-tier routing to the smallest model lowers average cost, but it does nothing about the serial depth causing the SLA miss under peak volume.
whyWrong.B: An alert on a breach reports the failure after it happens; it does not remove the serial dependency that causes the SLA to be missed.
whyWrong.D: A case-by-case agent's cost is a distribution, not a point; its tail can breach both the cost ceiling and the acknowledgment SLA under tripled volume.

t1Clause: must meet a stated six-hour acknowledgment SLA
